site.name: Belden Mining & Railroad Complex
site.category: Ghost Town / Railroad / Mining & Mill Complex
overview: Belden developed in the narrow Eagle River canyon below Battle Mountain as a railroad, mining, and ore-handling center serving the mines above Gilman.

The Denver & Rio Grande station, mining settlement, mills, load-out facilities, waste-rock structures, and railroad corridor created a dense industrial landscape linking the mountain mines with regional transportation.

timeline.text: Historic mapping identified Belden in the canyon and recorded it as a Denver & Rio Grande railroad station.
Mining expanded around Belden, with period reports describing substantial underground work, ore shipments, and a large workforce.
Belden became an important canyon-floor component of the consolidated Eagle Mine system, including mill and load-out infrastructure.
The area became part of the Eagle Mine Superfund cleanup, including stabilization of historic waste-rock cribbings and other mine-affected features.

features.name: Belden Townsite & Station Area
features.note: The historic settlement and railroad station occupied the narrow canyon floor.

features.name: Mill & Load-Out Area
features.note: Ore-processing and loading facilities connected Battle Mountain mining with the railroad.

features.name: Waste-Rock Cribbings
features.note: Large timber and later stabilization structures retain extensive historic mine waste along the canyon.

moreHistory: Belden's position at river and railroad level made it a natural transfer point for mines located high on Battle Mountain. Ore, supplies, workers, and equipment moved through the canyon while the railroad connected the district to smelters and markets.

By the early 1890s period accounts described intensive operation at the Belden Mine, including multiple work shifts and substantial ore shipments. Those figures are best understood as contemporary reports rather than audited lifetime production totals.

During the twentieth century the canyon became increasingly integrated with the Eagle Mine system. Mill, load-out, railroad, and waste-rock features combined to form one of the district's most important industrial corridors.

The surviving canyon landscape remains heavily shaped by mining and later environmental stabilization, making the relationship between railroad engineering, ore handling, mine waste, and steep terrain especially visible.
